title: California Clashes with DOJ Over Last-Minute Noncitizen Voting Probe
snippet: Top California officials are fiercely pushing back against a Justice Department demand to verify 20,000 voters within 48 hours, calling the effort a politically motivated attempt to disenfranchise voters ahead of the midterms.
content:
With less than two weeks remaining before the midterm elections, California officials are fiercely resisting a U.S. Department of Justice demand to verify the citizenship status of roughly 20,000 voters within a strict 48-hour deadline.

State leaders labeled the sudden federal oversight directive an attempt to politicize law enforcement and intimidate eligible voters shortly before Election Day.

State Leaders Push Back Against Federal Demand

California Attorney General Rob Bonta forcefully criticized the federal government's directive, accusing prosecutors of acting under explicit political motivation.

"It is once again the United States Department of Justice politicizing and weaponizing the law to attack its enemies, and it is completely improper," Bonta said during a recent broadcast interview. He emphasized that federal authorities provided a list of targeted individuals without offering substantive evidence regarding their supposed ineligibility.

Local election personnel in Los Angeles further raised red flags, noting that a high percentage of the names on the federal government's list were actually native-born U.S. citizens. California Governor Gavin Newsom publicly condemned the push as well, asserting on social media that the federal list included voters registered in the wrong counties as well as individuals who had never cast a ballot.

DOJ Charges Foreign Nationals Amid Escalating Legal Battle

The Justice Department defended its actions, stating that the request aimed to ensure election security in collaboration with the Department of Homeland Security. The federal push comes alongside recent charges filed against 28 foreign nationals—specifically lawful permanent residents—who were accused of fraudulently registering to vote.

"Today's arrests prove what we have been saying," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement. "California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote."

Despite the federal pressure, several California county officials declined to act on the last-minute demands, citing the proximity to the upcoming election and concerns over voter disenfranchisement. The dispute has now escalated into a legal battle, with a federal appeals court set to hear oral arguments on Tuesday.
